definition: A habitat (biome or ecosystem) that is primarily situated on or influenced by a landmass.
A mixture of varying proportions of sand, silt, clay, organic material, minerals, (aequous) liquids and gases, supporting the life of macro- and microorganisms in terrestrial habitats
A dry terrestrial habitat, characterized by low annual precipitation and/or high evaporation. Includes in particular desert areas.
comment: In MICRONT, this term is used as an additional qualifier for terrestrial habitats.

definition: A terrestrial ecosystem dominated by grasses.
A grassland ecosystem primarly shaped by grazing livestock.
A terrestrial ecosystem shaped by the (agricultural) cultivation of crops, including mechanical impacts such as active tilling.
A terrestrial ecosystem dominated by a dense population of trees and/or shrubs.
comment: includes woodland

definition: A cold and dry terrestrial ecosystem with low average temperatures, low precipitation (and/or high evaporation), dominated by low-growing vegetation (i.e., trees are moslty absent).
A terrestrial habitat (soil or rock) with temperatures constantly remaining below freezing point.
A terrestrial, semi-aquatic ecosystem that is usually inundated in gorund or surface water, including e.g. marshes and swamps.
A wetland habitat with saline conditions, often located in coastal areas.
A coastal wetland habitat dominated by mangrove trees.
A wetland ecosystem dominated by the accumulation of acidic peat,

A natural or anthropogenic subsurface habitat, including caves and mines, but also aquifers and geological features like (deep) deposits. Not strictly limited to landmass, but also includes features underneath lake/stream beds and below the ocean floor.
comment: More inclusive definition than ENVO:00002184 (subsurface landform)

definition: A solid aggregation of minerals (and mineraloids), potentially supporting growth in epilithic (on the rock surface) or endolithic (within the rock) habitats.
comment: In MICRONT, this term is used as an additional qualifier for terrestrial habitats to both specify areas or ecosystems dominated by rocks, and/or to the environmental material itself (e.g., supporting epilithic or endolithic growth).

definition: A habitat (biome or ecosystem) that is primarily dominated by water.
comment: In MICRONT, this term is used both for aquatic habitats and as an additional qualifier e.g. for aquatic hosts (like fish) or habitats influenced by, but not primarily dominated by water, such as wetlands

definition: An aquatic ecosystem determined by fresh water, i.e. a water body of low salinity (<0.5 ppt)
A lentic (still) water body containing predominantly fresh water
comment: Note: saline (and other non-fresh water) lakes are not included under this term; in MICRONT, these would be described as lentic water body (MICRONT:02060100) with the appropriate qualifiers

definition: Ground surface, interface and benthic layer of a lacustrine (lentic) fresh water body.
comment: In MICRONT, this term encompasses the water layer immediately above the solid ground layer. It is also restricted to fresh water systems; other lake beds are described via a combination of appropriate terms (e.g., saline, lentic water body and benthic)

definition: A lotic (flowing) water body containing predominantly fresh water. Includes streams and rivers.
comment: Note: saline (and other non-fresh water) streams are not included under this term, nor are springs; in MICRONT, these would be described as lotic water body (MICRONT:02060200) with the appropriate qualifiers

definition: Ground surface, interface and benthic layer of a fluvial (lotic) fresh water body.
comment: In MICRONT, this term encompasses the water layer immediately above the solid ground layer. It is also restricted to fresh water systems; other stream beds are described via a combination of appropriate terms (e.g., lotic water body and benthic)

definition: An aquatic ecosystem primarily determined by marine (ocean or sea) water. This ranges from littoral/coastal to open ocean habitats, as well as from surface water to seafloor.
comment: Note: while most marine waters are saline (e.g., meet the criteria for high salinity, MICRONT:09010103), many marine habitats are indeed dominated by medium salinity (brackish) or very high salinity (briny) water.

definition: Ground surface, interface and immediate benthic layer at the bottom of a marine water body
A ground surface feature where water can flow out of the ground. Includes terrestrial springs, as well as aquatic features (such as underwater seeps or vents)
A terrestrial spring where hot (geothermally heated) water flows from the ground.
A marine spring where hot (geothermally heated) water flows from fissures in the seafloord.
A spring where water emerges through permeable ground layers. Includes cold seeps (at ocean floors) and terrestrial seeps (often associated with wetlands).
An aquatic ecosystem determined by water of intermediate (medium) salinity, broadly in the range of 0.5-30ppt
comment: medium salinity (0.5-30ppt)

definition: An aquatic ecosystem at the interface at stream mouths, i.e. the outflow of streams into the sea. Generally determined by brackish water, or the (tidal) mixing of saline and fresh water.
An aquatic ecosystem determined by water of high salinity, i.e. in the range of 30-50ppt
comment: high salinity (30-50 ppt)

definition: An aquatic habitat determined by water of very high, including near-saturating, concentrations of salt (>=50 ppt)
comment: very high salinity (>=50 ppt)

definition: A habitat determined by water that is frozen solid.
A still (non-flowing) water body
A water body with (directed) flow)
Water contained in (subsurface) rock pores or deposits.
comment: In MICRONT, this term also more broadly includes aquifers.

definition: Deposits formed at the bottom of water bodies via the deposition (sedimentation) of particles from the liquid phase.
comment: In MICRONT, this term specifically refers to sediments in extant water bodies, not to remnant sediments that resulted from former (e.g., dried up) water bodies.

definition: Near-shore (coastal) zone of a water body, at the terrestrial-aquatic interface; includes near-shore terrestrial zone as well (i.e., zones that are occasionally inundated and/or directly influenced by the adjacent water body)
comment: In MICRONT, this term includes both the aquatic and terrestrial near-shore zone.

definition: Open water zone of a water body, neither near the shore nor near the bed.
comment: In MICRONT, this term is used as a qualifier and can be used to describe either marine or lake pelagic waters.

definition: Topmost layer of a water body, extending from the surface to around 200m depth, i.e. as deep as sunlight penetrates to a degree that allows photosynthesis
Twilight zone of a water body where <1% of sunlight penetrates, extending roughly from 200-1000m depth
Midnight zone of open ocean water, extending from depths of 1000-2500m (only few lakes are in this depth range)
Deep marine open water layer extending from a depth of 2500m to roughly 6000m, or to within 100m of the seafloor
Open water within deep marine trenches, at depths >6000m
The bottom layer of a water body, close to its bed and including the upper layers of the ground that are directly influenced by the water body above.
The aquatic part of a wetland ecosystem
comment: In MICRONT, paludal is used as an extra qualifier to specifically refer to the aquatic part (i.e., not the sediment or soil) of a wetland ecosystem.

definition: A microbial habitat that is directly determined by a host organism in terms of physical, abiotic and biotic parameters.
comment: In MICRONT, host-association is considered based on physical (growth on, in or in direct proximity to the host) and biotic/metabolic (growth directly depending on conditions determined by the host) parameters. Only multicellular eukaryotes are considered as host organisms; associations among bacteria, archaea and unicellular eukaryotes (even including intracellular growth) are not included under this umbrella term. A host-associated lifestlye is considered as opposed to a free-living lifestyle.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a green plant host (NCBI tax ID 33090, Viridiplantae).
comment: In MICRONT, host-association is considered based on physical (growth on, in or in direct proximity to the host) and biotic/metabolic (growth directly depending on conditions determined by the host) parameters. Plant-associated habitats do not include plant-derived products, such as foods (fruit, etc.), wood or processed products (such as paper, etc).

definition: A habitat directly determined by plant roots, encompassing both root tissues (i.e., the endorhizosphere) and the region directly adjacent to roots which is influenced by plant secretions.
comment: In MICRONT, a broad definition is used to include both the roots themselves and the region immediately adjacent. Elsewhere, rhizosphere is often defined more narrowly to only include root-adjacent soil or substrate (e.g. ENVO:00005801)

definition: A habitat directly determined by non-root parts of a plant, e.g. above-ground tissues like leaves and flowers, but also the stem.
Dead plant material (primarily leaves, bark, twigs, etc) that has fallen to the ground.
comment: Does not include (dropped) fruit.

definition: A habitat directly determined by an animal host (NCBI tax ID 33208, Metazoa).
comment: In MICRONT, host-association is considered based on physical (growth on, in or in direct proximity to the host) and biotic/metabolic (growth directly depending on conditions determined by the host) parameters. Animal-associated environments do not include animal-derived products, like food products (dairy, meat, etc) or processed products such as leather, etc.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a mammalian host (NCBI tax ID 40674, Mammalia)
A habitat directly determined by a porcine host (NCBI tax ID 40674, Suidae, i.e. swine)
comment: Suidae correspond to swine, including pigs, hogs, etc.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a primate host (NCBI tax ID 9443, Primates)
comment: This includes lemurs, monkeys, apes (including humans), etc.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a human host (NCBI tax ID 9606, Homo sapiens)
A habitat directly determined by a ruminant host (NCBI tax ID 9845, Ruminantia)
comment: Includes herbivores whose digestive system includes a rumen, but the definition is based on taxonom (suborder Ruminantia). Members include cervids (deer), bovids (like cattle, sheep, goats and antelopes), and giraffes.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a bovine host (NCBI tax ID 27592, Bovinae).
comment: Includes cattle, bison, buffalo and certain types of antelopes.

definition: A habitat direclty determined by a cervid host (NCBI tax ID 9850, Cervidae, i.e. deer)
A habitat directly determined by an ovine host (NCBI tax ID 9935, genus Ovis, i.e. sheep)
A habitat direclty determined by a caprine host (NCBI tax ID 9922, genus Capra, i.e. goats iand ibex, but not including other caprines like sheep etc)
A habitat directly determined by a carnivore host (NCBI tax ID 33554, Carnivora)
comment: Definition is based on phylogeny, not on carnivorous dietary habits, although most Carnivora are indeed carnivorous. Group includes dogs, cats, bears, seals, otters, etc

definition: A habitat directly determined by a canine host (NCBI tax ID 9608, Canidae)
comment: Includes dogs, wolves, coyotes and foxes. Note: tax ID more broadly corresponds to family Canidae, but only extant subfamily are Caninae.

definition: A habitat direclty determined by a feline host (NCBI tax ID 9681, Felidae)
comment: Includes cats and panthers. Note: tax ID more broadly corresponds to family Felidae, but only extant subfamily is Felinae (which includes cats and panthers).

definition: A habitat directly determined by an ursine host (NCBI tax ID 9632, Ursidae, i.e. bears)
comment: Note: family Ursidae includes bears (Ursinae), as well as short-faced bears and pandas.

definition: A habitat direclty determined by a reptilian host (NCBI tax ID 32561, Sauria; see comment)
comment: Given unclear taxonomy of the group Reptilia, the NCBI taxonomy is used where tax ID Sauria includes all reptilian groups, including birds.

definition: A habitat directly determined by an avian host (NCBI tax ID 8782, Aves, i.e. birds)
A habitat directly determined by an insect host (NCBI tax ID 50557, Insecta)
A habitat directly determined by a tick host (NCBI tax ID 69335, Ixodida)
A habitat direcly determined by a ray-finned fish host (NCBI tax ID 7898, Actinopterygii; see comment)
comment: Includes ray-finned fishes, but neither cartilaginous fishes (like sharks, rays) nor Sarcopterygii (which would include lungfish and extant groups mammals, reptiles and amphibians and therefore introduce unintended annotations with misleading ecological implications)

definition: A habitat direclty determined by a mollusc host (tax ID 7898, Mollusca)
comment: Includes bivalves (mussels, clams, etc), gastropods (snails, slugs, etc), cephalopods (squid, octopus, etc), and further groups within the phylum Mollusca. As more respective data comes in, additional subcategories for these groups may be introduced in MICRONT in the future

definition: A habitat directly determined by a coral host (tax ID 6101, Anthrozoa)
comment: More broadly includes coral reef habitats, i.e. not only habitats directly physically located on or in a coral host, but including the immediate surroundings.

definition: A habitat directly determined by a sponge host (tax ID 6040, Porifera)
comment: More broadly includes not only habitats directly physically located on or in sponge tissue, but also immediate surroundings.

definition: A habitat directly determined by an amphibian host (tax ID 8292, Amphibia)
comment: Includes frogs, salamanders, etc

definition: A habitat directly determined by a digestive tract, i.e. an animal's anatomical and physiological system for the digestion of food.
A habitat directly determined by an oral cavity.
comment: Includes tongue, teeth, etc, but also secretions (saliva) and accretions (dental plaque, etc).

definition: A bodily fluid secreted from specialized glands in the oral cavity. Usually involved in initial digestion steps, e.g. catalysing the breakdown of starch.
Paleontological sample of calculus, i.e. accretions of multiple layers of hardened dental plaque.
Hollow organ as part of a digestive tract, involved in the gastric phase of digestion, i.e. breakdown of food via secreted digestive enzymes and often via acidification.
A specialized stomach in ruminants, involved in the breakdown of food including structural carbohydrates (such as celluloses) under the participation of microbial communities
comment: Note: although the rumen is anatomically a stomach, its physiology is so different from other gastric organs that it is considered as a separate category (and not a subcategory of stomachs) in MICRONT.

definition: A series of specialized organs in the lower gastrointestinal tract, involved in the further digestion of chyme exiting from the stomach. The intestine generally spans from the exit of the stomach to the anus or rectum.
Solid or semisolid of non-digested food and shed host cells, excreted via the anus.
Primary sex organs of the reproductive system and organs of the urinary system.
Organ of the female reproductive tract in mammals.
Respiratory tract organs in mammals, spanning from nasal cavity to lung.
comment: Note: in MICRONT, use is currently restricted to mammalian airways, as samples from non-mammalian animals are not (yet) prevalent in repositories.

definition: Habitat provided by the flexible outer tissue covering the body of a vertebrate animal.
Liquids produced and/or secreted by animal bodies.
Milk produced in the mammary glands of women. Definition in the narrow sense, i.e. restricted to human breast milk.
comment: refers to human breast milk only; note that milk of other mammals as (processed) food stuff is annotated as anthropogenic:food:dairy product

definition: Bodily fluid in vertebrates that transports nutrients, oxygen, metabolic waste products and body cells (including immune cells) within a circulatory system.
Bodily fluid surrounding meningeal tissues in parts of the brain and along the spinal cord.
Membraneous layer covering internal organs and lining cavities within an animal, e.g. within the mouth, nose, lung, gut or vagina.
A habitat directly determined by an animal's eye, i.e. a primary visual sensual organ.
A habitat that is directly and primarily determined by the impact of human activity, in particular in terms of its physical, chemical and biotic makeup.

A biological sample that is not directly derived from an environmental or host-associated microbial habitat, or which has been processed to intenionally skew the taxonomic or functional composition relative to a sample of origin.
comment: In MICRONT, this category includes laboratory experiments, mock communities, negative and positive control samples, spike-in experiments, cultivation and enrichment designs, sorted cells, and others.

definition: An artificial sample with a predefined mix of organisms, used as reference or for laboratory experiments.
An artificial sample that should not contain any microbes, or that was obtained to establish a baseline for microbial contamination control.
comment: Note: in MICRONT this term refers exclusively to sampling control (e.g., swabs only or extraction buffers without biological input material); it does *not* encompass negative controls in a study design sense, i.e. samples with a control treatment.

definition: An experimental setup within an environment where parameters like temperature and nutrient/gas availability can be actively controlled. Encompasses in particular cultivation experiments from real environmental samples, such as microcosm or mesocosm experiments.
A habitat directly determined by human-manufactured structures at macroscopic scales, e.g. buildings and public infrastructure (like roads, etc)
A building where healthcare services are provided to patients by specialized staff using specialized equipment.
Water impacted by human influence, e.g. following domestic, agricultural or industrial uses.
comment: In MICRONT, this term to be used as generic default when more specific info is not available

definition: Unprocessed domestic wastewater (before reaching a treatment plant), usually containing urine and feces.
Semi-solid slurry that remains after wastewater treatment.
comment: Includes also activated sludge (ENVO:00002046)

definition: A habitat that is directly determined or influenced by agricultural activity, i.e. crop or livestock farming.
comment: In MICRONT, the term is primarily used as an additional qualifier, e.g. to specify that a soil (MICRONT:01010000) is indeed an agricultural soil. Also includes aquaculture samples.

definition: A habitat that is primarily determined by (annual) crop species and agricultural activity.
Animal feces that are used as organic fertilizer in agriculture.
comment: Note: in MICRONT, this term explicitly only encompasses animal manure; compost or green manure are considered in a separate category (MICRONT:04070100) as they are procedurally similar (used as fertilizers), but ecologically and microbiologically very distinct.

definition: A habitat primarily determined by anthropogenic excavations at or below the Earth's surface for the extraction of minerals.
Any substance consumed for nutritional purposes. Includes unprocessed (e.g., raw fruit and vegetables) and processed (e.g., fermented or cooked) food.
comment: In MICRONT, the term primarily refers to food for human consumption, not e.g. feed for livestock or food sources for wild animals (like krill for whales, etc)

definition: Processed food where carbohydrates have been metabolized under (mostly) anaerobic conditions by microorganisms.
comment: Includes in particular lactic acid, alcohol and acetic acid fermentation, among others.

definition: Food product derived from mammalian milk, usually cow, sheep, goat or mare's milk.
Processed dairy product based on coagulated and fermented milk.
Food product derived from animal tissue, usually muscle.
Undesired or unusable material discarded as the result of human activity, but excluding humans bodily excreta.
Decomposing plant or food waste, generally used as fertilizer in agriculture.
comment: Note: does not include plant litter (MICRONT:03010300) which specifically to dead plant material that has fallen to the ground where it may also decompose, but not in a human-impacted process like composting. Also not associated with the term manure (MICRONT:04040200) which in MICRONT refers to animal manure only, even though compost and green manure are functionally similar in that all are generally used as fertilizer.

definition: Aerial habitats, including aerosol particles and other airborne particulate matter.

definition: very low or no oxygen; O2 concentration <0.5 mg/L
An aggregation of microorganisms, usually a community of distinct species, embedded with a secreted extracellular matrix. Generally adherent to a solid substrate.
A multi-layered, complex biofilm of microorganisms; can be up to several cm thick.
Wild animals, not held or bred in captivity
Captive animals (e.g. in a zoo), but not domesticated
Domesticated animals, i.e. in close dependence to humans, bred over multiple generations
comment: includes domesticated animals

definition: Companion animals living in close association with humans, usually within a household and with constant (social) interactions with humans
Human infant, aged 0-2 years
Human child, aged >2 to 10 years
Human adolescent, aged >10 to <18 years
Human adult, aged 18 to 65 years
Human elderly, aged >65 years
Born at <37 weeks gestational age (for humans)
Born at ≥37 weeks gestational age (for humans)
subject lives in an urban area (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area)
subject lives in a rural area (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area)
Lifestyle dominated by products and services provided by the use of (industrial) machines and technology

Lifestyle not majorly impacted by products and services resulting from the use of industrial machines and technology; this includes in particular food production and processing, domestic living conditions (including sanitation) and transport
Non-industrialized lifestyle where food is primarily obtained by foraging, i.e. not relying on agriculture or animal husbandry

Non-industrialized lifestyle where food is primarily obtained from traditional agriculture, i.e. procuded in small lots without relying on industrial machines and technology; this includes pastoralism.
Palaeontological samples from preserved microbial communities, e.g. from ancient dental calculus or mummified tissues
impacted by a contaminant, e.g. chemical or radioactive; does not refer to laboratory contamination (introduced e.g. via extraction kits)
